summary: Describes the IANA table that says how X.400 message body part types match MIME content types, and sets up its initial contents. New mappings were meant to be registered with IANA to avoid duplicates. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Two people speak different languages. This memo is a translation chart that tells which word in one language means the same as a word in the other.

questions: x.400 to mime body type equivalence

subtitle: A lookup table for gateways that translate message bodies between X.400 mail and Internet MIME mail.

tldr.problem: Gateways between X.400 mail and MIME-based RFC-822 mail need an agreed way to say which X.400 body part type corresponds to which MIME content-type, and how to convert between them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the IANA MHS/MIME Equivalence table, with one entry per pair giving the X.400 body part, the MIME content-type, a conversion type and optional comments. It fills in the initial entries and defines new body parts and content-types where none existed.
tldr.outcome: New mappings were meant to be registered with IANA to limit duplication. The RFC is now Historic.

today: RFC 1494 is Historic, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It was written as a companion to RFC 1495.

sections.title: Purpose of the Equivalence Table
sections.content:
RFC 1494 is a companion to RFC 1495, which sets out the principles for interworking between MIME-based RFC-822 mail and X.400 mail. This memo describes the content of the IANA MHS/MIME Equivalence table that RFC 1495 refers to, and defines the table's initial contents.

The two worlds use different words. MIME calls an information object in a message body a content-type; X.400 calls it a body part type. The memo uses body part for either. Mappings for new content-types or body part types should be registered with IANA to minimize redundancy and promote interoperability.
sections.eli5: Two mail systems name the same kinds of attachments differently. This memo is the shared dictionary that says which name matches which.

sections.title: Table Entries and Conversion Types
sections.content:
Each MIME content-type and X.400 body part pair gets one table entry with four parts: the X.400 Body Part (with any OBJECT IDENTIFIERs needed to identify it), the MIME Content-Type (which must already be registered with IANA), the Conversion Type, and optional Comments. Future submissions to IANA are to follow the same format.

There are four generic conversion types:

  • Byte copy: no conversion at all. The byte stream is copied as is. This is the preferred conversion, and implementors are strongly encouraged to define formats so that a gateway can use it.
  • Text conversion: for text that cannot be byte-copied, for example because of different encodings of nonstandard characters or of line and page breaks.
  • Image conversion: for raster images such as Group 3 Facsimile or JPEG, working on pixels rather than characters.
  • Tunneling: an encapsulation, not a conversion. It is the fallback when no explicit mapping applies.
sections.eli5: Each line in the chart says what to do with an attachment: copy it as is, tidy up the text or picture, or, if nothing fits, wrap it in a package and send it along.

sections.title: New Body Parts and Content-Types
sections.content:
Where no mapping existed, the memo defines new ones. All new X.400 body parts are Extended Body Parts as defined in X.420. They are identified by OBJECT IDENTIFIERs under mime-mhs-bodies, with one subtree for data (mime-mhs-bp-data) and one for parameters (mime-mhs-bp-parameter).

A generic MIME Extended Body Part carries any MIME content-type that has no registered mapping. To convert, the gateway copies the type/subtype string and each parameter into a MimeParameters structure, reverses the transfer encoding to get the original bytes, and puts those bytes in the data octet string. Dedicated body parts are also defined for PostScript, JPEG and GIF, each with no parameters.

In the other direction, the new MIME content-type application/x400-bp carries any X.400(88) body part with no registered mapping. Its bp-type parameter is the body part's tag number for a basic body part, or the OBJECT IDENTIFIER for an extended one. Base64 is recommended as the transfer encoding if the content cannot be inspected first.
sections.eli5: When the chart has no entry, the memo says to put the attachment in a plain labeled box that both systems know how to open.

sections.title: Mapping Details for Text, Fax and ODA
sections.content:
Section 7 gives the entry for each pair. IA5Text maps to text/plain with US-ASCII by byte copy; the RFC converts the IA5 "currency" symbol to the "dollar" symbol without comment. GeneralText maps to text/plain with an ISO-8859 charset by byte copy, using a table from MIME charsets to ISO registry numbers; if there is no match, the generic body part is used instead.

The g3-facsimile body part maps to a new image/g3fax content-type with parameters page-length, page-width, encoding, resolution, DCS and pages. Pages are separated by a sequence of six EOL markers, each EOL being eleven zeroes and a one. The ODA body part maps to application/oda with profile and class parameters; if either is missing, Q112 and formatted-processable are assumed.

For BilaterallyDefined and application/octet-stream, the RFC notes that the conversion fails when parameters are present, and that BilaterallyDefined body parts are deprecated in both 1988 and 1992 X.400 and kept only for compatibility with 1984 systems.
sections.eli5: Each kind of attachment gets its own small recipe. A fax is cut into pages using a special marker, and plain text is mostly copied straight across.

sections.title: Registering New Mappings
sections.content:
Section 9 gives an e-mail registration form for IANA. It asks for the MIME type name (already registered with IANA), the X.400 body part, the OBJECT IDENTIFIERs for data and parameters (IANA assigns them under the two subtrees if left empty), the ASN.1 syntax, the conversion algorithm and a contact. The algorithm must be defined completely enough for independent implementation, and may refer to RFCs. Accepted registrations were to be listed in the "Assigned Numbers" series of RFCs.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: If someone invents a new attachment type, they fill in a form so the shared dictionary gets a new line for it.
